Only about 5 million of Thailand's 27 million borrowers are financially healthy and qualify to access additional credit, said former chief of the National Credit Bureau Surapol Opasatien, leaving millions at risk of falling into long-term debt distress and legal proceedings. FALLING INCOME, RISING DEBT Told about struggling debtors like Kavita, Thailand's Finance Minister Ekniti Nitithanprapas pointed to the country's rock-bottom interest rate of [USN:L6N44N0DW TEXT:"1%"] and ongoing co-operation with the central bank and lenders to manage the issue. "We need to make sure that household debt will be addressed by the rising income of the people," he told Reuters, outlining [USN:L6N45H0M5 TEXT:"a plan to hit 3% GDP growth"] within three years by drawing foreign investments into key sectors like semiconductors. That's still less than the 5% GDP growth Surapol estimates is required to bring Thailand's household debt-to-GDP ratio to under 80% — a tipping point where negative debt effects intensify. For Kavita, who has one daughter studying medicine and another in middle school, it is a daily fight to find enough money to keep her household running. "I still don't see the light at the end of the tunnel," she said. "My life will probably end before the debts are fully repaid." ($1 = 33.55 baht)

item.title: Asia shares slip, bonds submerged in tide of AI debt
item.description: Asian shares slid on Thursday as strains in sovereign bond markets were aggravated by reports some major tech companies were seeking to raise billions in debt in direct competition for limited funding.
item.dc:creator: Wayne Cole
item.content:encoded: Asian shares slid on Thursday as strains in sovereign bond markets were aggravated by reports some major [USN:FWN45T25Y TEXT:"tech companies"] were seeking to raise billions in debt in direct competition for limited funding. Oil prices jumped anew amid an increase in [USN:L1N45U01Q TEXT:"attacks on shipping"] in the Gulf and added to the pressure on Treasuries, even as a strong auction of US 10-year debt overnight helped pull yields back from 24-year peaks. While lofty yields underpinned the dollar, the euro slid to near 17-month lows as concerns over [USN:L1N45T0KZ TEXT:"France's finances"] spread to Italian and Greek debt. The steady climb in borrowing costs put equities on the defensive and Japan's Nikkei (.N225) skidded 1.1%, while South Korea (.KS11) slumped 2.1%. MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan (.MIAPJ0000PUS) shed 1.2%. On Wall Street, S&P 500 futures and Nasdaq futures both dipped 0.1%. In Europe, EUROSTOXX 50 futures , DAX futures and FTSE futures were all flat after sliding on Wednesday. In commodity markets, Brent futures rose 2.1% to $102.30 a barrel, while US crude futures added 1.7% to $89.79 a barrel. The Wall Street Journal added to media reports that SpaceX (SPCX.O) , Broadcom (AVGO.O) and Oracle (ORCL.N) were looking to raise money to buy AI chips. Broadcom was looking for $50 billion in financing, while [USN:L6N45S1CR TEXT:"SpaceX"] was planning to issue $30 billion in investment-grade debt and raise $10 billion in loans to buy chips from Nvidia (NVDA.O) , which is a major shareholder in SpaceX. The news saw credit default insurance on SpaceX jump to record highs, while its shares and bonds lost ground. Nigel Green, CEO of deVere Group, warned of a dangerous loop where Nvidia was bankrolling the very customers who buy its products, leaving global investors at risk if the expected profits failed to materialise. "The AI build-out started on cash," said Green. "It's increasingly running on credit, and credit changes the risk profile entirely." "Debt has to be repaid on schedule, whether the revenues show up or not," he added. "And this debt is landing in the bond funds and pension pots of savers right around the world.” SOVEREIGN BONDS VS CORPORATE DEBT Still, the fact much of this money will be spent on AI equipment could be positive for earnings in the semiconductor and memory sectors. Samsung Electronics (005930.KS) on Thursday projected a 783% jump in third-quarter operating profit to 107.4 trillion won ($80.17 billion), though its shares lost 1.2%. All this corporate debt is coming at a time when sovereign bond markets are being sorely tested by inflation fears, ever-widening budget deficits and rising cash rates. Minutes of the [USN:L6N45T0TQ TEXT:"Federal Reserve's"] last meeting released on Wednesday showed "most" members considered another rate hike likely by year-end, though they would approach each meeting with an open mind. Markets imply just a 19% chance the Fed will move again this month, but are 80% priced for a rise in December. "We expect a second Fed hike in December, though we see a strong chance the Fed ultimately concludes further tightening is unnecessary," wrote analysts at Goldman Sachs in a note. The prospect of a pause in tightening helped keep 2-year Treasury yields at 4.78% , while 10-year yields crept up to 5.3019% , having hit a 24-year top of 5.326% overnight. Strains in the French bond market led [USN:L8N45T074 TEXT:"Bank of France head Emmanuel Moulin"] to acknowledge the country's economic situation was serious, but said it did not need help from the European Central Bank. Investors reacted by dumping the euro, which was pinned at $1.1204 after having lost 0.6% overnight. A break of the recent low at $1.1161 would risk a retreat to $1.1065. The dollar was the main beneficiary of the single currency's woes and its index rose to 102.22 , near an 18-month peak. It was steady on the yen at 158.10 , with the Japanese currency protected by the threat of intervention. Non-interest-bearing gold has suffered as yields climbed, but managed a modest 0.6% bounce to $4,136 an ounce having found bids at two-month lows.

item.title: Dollar steady near 18-month high after Fed minutes flag inflation risks
item.description: The dollar held near its strongest level in 18 months in subdued trading in Asia on Thursday, after hawkish minutes from the US Federal Open Market Committee signalled policymakers viewed inflation as the biggest risk to their outlook.
item.dc:creator: Gregor Hunter
item.content:encoded: The dollar held near its strongest level in 18 months in subdued trading in Asia on Thursday, after [USN:L6N45T0TQ TEXT:"hawkish minutes"] from the US Federal Open Market Committee signalled policymakers viewed inflation as the biggest risk to their outlook. The dollar index , which measures its strength against a basket of six currencies, was steady at 102.25 after rising 0.3% on Wednesday. The greenback remains within a few pips of its strongest levels since April 9, 2025, following the market turmoil that accompanied the so-called Liberation Day tariff announcement the previous week. Federal Reserve policymakers voted unanimously to raise interest rates by a quarter of a percentage point at the US central bank's September 15-16 meeting, but minutes released on Wednesday indicated divisions over their rationale for doing so. "The FOMC’s minutes reinforced the hawkish tone accompanying the Fed’s September rate hike, with most participants still viewing further tightening as appropriate and almost all seeing inflation risks tilted to the upside at the time of the meeting," Westpac analysts wrote. The yield on the US 10-year Treasury bond was up 3 basis points at 5.303%. "The continued sell-off in US Treasuries is becoming an increasingly important driver for global markets," MUFG analysts wrote. "Should long-end yields rise further, market attention could shift towards the broader tightening in US financial conditions and whether policymakers begin to signal greater concern over Treasury-market conditions." Still, the minutes did little to shift expectations that the Fed will stand pat at its meeting later this month. Fed funds futures are pricing an implied 81.7% probability the US central bank will keep rates on hold at its next two-day meeting ending October 28, nudging up from 80.1% a day earlier, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool. Against the yen , the US dollar was up 0.1% at 158.18 yen, reversing a short-lived dip after data released on Thursday showed Japan's [USN:P8N44I065 TEXT:"current account surplus"] stood at 4.062 trillion yen ($25.7 billion) in August, higher than economists' median forecast for a surplus of 3.19 trillion yen. The Australian dollar was down 0.1% at $0.6955, while its kiwi counterpart was flat at $0.5602. Against the Chinese yuan , the US dollar was flat at 6.7035 yuan in offshore trade. The euro was up 0.1% at $1.1202, while the British pound was unchanged at $1.3212. Bitcoin fell 1.3% to $82,360.17, while ether was 0.8% lower at $2,554.41.

item.title: Shell, Chevron cut Gulf of Mexico output as Tropical Storm Isaias approaches
item.description: Shell and Chevron said on Wednesday they were curtailing offshore operations in the Gulf of Mexico as Tropical Storm Isaias approached the region.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Shell (SHEL.L) and Chevron (CVX.N) said on Wednesday they were curtailing offshore operations in the Gulf of Mexico as Tropical Storm Isaias approached the region. Shell said it was evacuating all personnel and shutting in production at its Mars, Olympus, Ursa, Vito and Appomattox assets. The company added that it had already moved non-essential personnel from its Stones asset. Separately, Chevron said it had initiated shut-in procedures for production at four Chevron-operated Gulf of Mexico facilities in preparation for the storm. The US oil major added that some additional personnel were being transported onshore, while production at its other five Gulf of America, referring to the Gulf of Mexico, facilities remained at normal levels. [USN:L6N45T0WN TEXT:"Tropical Storm Isaias"] formed in the Gulf of Mexico on Wednesday and is forecast to strengthen into a hurricane before slamming into the southern US coast early on Saturday, bringing heavy rains, storm surges, and possible tornadoes across several states, the National Hurricane Center said.

item.title: Bezos says Blue Origin likely to pursue IPO in coming years
item.description: Blue Origin is likely to pursue an initial public offering in the coming years, billionaire founder Jeff Bezos said on Wednesday, after the space company raised $10 billion from outside investors for the first time in a funding round.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Blue Origin is likely to pursue an initial public offering in the coming years, billionaire founder Jeff Bezos said on Wednesday, after the space company raised $10 billion from outside investors for the first time in a funding round. "I think, someday, Blue Origin will have an IPO... It would be several years from now. But it probably makes sense for Blue Origin to be a public company at some point," Bezos said on FOX News Channel's "Special Report with Bret Baier". The remarks are Bezos' clearest indication yet that Blue Origin could seek a stock market listing. An eventual IPO would offer investors exposure to a major space company amid renewed interest in the sector, though rival SpaceX (SPCX.O) , which listed in June, remains the dominant player. Bezos, who also founded Amazon.com (AMZN.O) , said he has personally invested $28 billion in Blue Origin since establishing the company in 2000. The Wall Street Journal reported in September that Blue Origin's recent [USN:L4N43A14C TEXT:"funding round"] valued it at $140 billion. Founded about 18 months before Elon Musk's SpaceX, Blue Origin has largely relied on Bezos for funding while securing multibillion-dollar NASA and US Space Force contracts, including for work on the Artemis lunar program. Blue Origin aims to resume New Glenn launches this year after a [USN:L1N442183 TEXT:"launch-pad explosion"] during a static-fire test in May delayed its efforts to compete with SpaceX in the commercial launch market. "December of this year, we're going to fly that vehicle again," Bezos said.

item.title: CrowdStrike says China-based suspect used AI tools in South Korean bank hacks
item.description: The suspect behind recent cyberattacks targeting South Korea's financial sector may be a 26-year-old based in China's Guangdong province who used a Chinese-developed AI agent tool called ARTEX and Anthropic's Claude Code, US cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike said.
item.dc:creator: Kyu-Seok Shim, Brenda Goh
item.content:encoded: The suspect behind recent cyberattacks targeting South Korea's financial sector may be a 26-year-old based in China's Guangdong province who used a Chinese-developed AI agent tool called ARTEX and Anthropic's Claude Code, US cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike said. In a report published on Wednesday, CrowdStrike (CRWD.O) said it uncovered personal details linked to the suspected attacker while analysing AI coding-tool sessions and infrastructure associated with a campaign [USN:L6N45S035 TEXT:"targeting"] South Korean financial institutions from late September to early October. The case is likely to intensify concerns over the rise of AI agents and whether organisations are prepared to defend their systems against them. Australia said last month that an [USN:L4N45F1EW TEXT:"OpenAI autonomous agent"] breached a government health statistics portal in June, marking one of the first known instances of an AI agent hacking a government system. CrowdStrike said the attacker used ARTEX, a recently released Chinese-developed open-source penetration testing tool, alongside large language models such as Claude. "While this activity has not been attributed to a named adversary, the threat actor is likely a Chinese speaker and financially motivated," it said. "This assessment is made with moderate confidence based on the use of the Chinese-developed tool ARTEX and observed Chinese-language prompts." BANK HACKS CrowdStrike said the individual also asked Claude where threat actors typically sell Korean data breach information and sought assistance in finding Korean Telegram data sales groups. In another session, the person also requested Claude to create a security researcher resume, which included details such as a Telegram account, age, educational background and a location in Maoming, a city in the southern Chinese province of Guangdong, which CrowdStrike said likely belonged to the attacker. A man who answered a phone number provided by CrowdStrike in its report said he had no knowledge of the matter. Anthropic, South Korean police and China's foreign ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment. ARTEX is an open-source AI agent for automated penetration testing that was published on GitHub this year by a Chinese security engineer with the handle Autumn. It is not a standalone large language model but connects to external LLMs such as ChatGPT, Claude and DeepSeek to help organisations test for vulnerabilities in the networks. The tool’s GitHub page says it is intended for personal learning, code research and local technical verification and should not be used to conduct real-world testing against online systems or websites. At least nine South Korean banks have disclosed or have been reported by local media as having been targeted by cyberattacks since late September, prompting South Korean police to launch a probe this week and President Lee Jae Myung to call for robust response measures. Shinhan Bank said last week that personal information of about 25,000 of its customers was compromised, while KB Kookmin Bank said that the personal information of 119 of its customers was leaked.

item.title: Samsung flags $80 billion profit on AI boom, highest quarterly for any tech company
item.description: Samsung Electronics on Thursday projected its quarterly profit would top 100 trillion won, a world first for a technology company, estimating a nearly nine-fold jump in third-quarter earnings as booming demand for AI chips drove strong memory sales.
item.dc:creator: Heekyong Yang, Hyunjoo Jin
item.content:encoded: Samsung Electronics (005930.KS) on Thursday projected its quarterly profit would top 100 trillion won, a world first for a technology company, estimating a nearly nine-fold jump in third-quarter earnings as booming demand for AI chips drove strong memory sales. The world's largest memory chipmaker estimated an operating profit of 107.4 trillion won ($80.17 billion) for the July-September period, slightly ahead of an LSEG SmartEstimate of 106.1 trillion won. The forecast marks Samsung's fourth straight quarter of record operating profit, underscoring a deepening global memory chip shortage as AI infrastructure investment outpaces supply growth, which has driven chip prices up sharply. Samsung and Micron (MU.O) expect the imbalance to persist into 2028, although Chinese competition and a potential slowdown in AI spending pose risks to the longer-term earnings outlook. Samsung's shares moved sideways despite flagging another record profit, slipping 0.2% in early trade versus a 0.5% fall in the benchmark KOSPI (.KS11) . Its share price has slumped more than 25% from a record high in June amid concerns about the durability of the AI boom. Analysts have also recently trimmed their forecasts due to the sharp appreciation of the South Korean currency, which reduces the value of dollar-denominated overseas sales when converted into local currency. "The market's focus has shifted to whether the sharp earnings growth that started a year ago would be sustainable," market analyst Kim Seok-hwan at Mirae Asset Securities said. Analysts expect profit in the fourth quarter to grow 8.2% from the previous quarter, slowing from 20% sequential quarterly growth in the third quarter, with chip price growth abating. Market research firm TrendForce expects conventional DRAM contract prices to rise 10% to 15% in the fourth quarter from the preceding quarter, much slower than a second-quarter surge of roughly 60%. The moderation in memory prices is being closely watched by investors after a more than year-long rally that propelled profit margins to record highs for the world's largest memory producers Samsung, SK Hynix (000660.KS) and Micron. Third-quarter revenue would likely rise 127% to 195 trillion won from a year earlier, Samsung said. The company will release detailed results, including a breakdown of earnings by business division, on October 29. BIGGER-THAN-EXPECTED MOBILE LOSS Memory chips are expected to account for the bulk of the earnings improvement. Prices have soared due to the tight supply of conventional DRAM and NAND chips as well as growing demand for high-bandwidth memory (HBM), essential for processing vast amounts of data for AI applications. Douglas Kim of Douglas Research Advisory estimated that Samsung's HBM bit shipments expanded by close to 50% quarter-over-quarter in the third quarter, with Samsung trying to narrow the gap with SK Hynix (000660.KS) in the HBM market. But the memory chip boom presents a challenge for Samsung's other businesses, particularly its smartphone and consumer electronics divisions, which face mounting pressure from higher component costs. Samsung's mobile business posted a larger-than-expected loss of more than $1 billion in the third quarter, analysts said. Meanwhile, Samsung's contract chipmaking, or foundry, business is expected to remain loss-making because of the burden of fixed costs and still-low utilisation rates, analysts said. However, utilisation is expected to improve over the next several quarters, supported by stronger demand for advanced manufacturing processes. Samsung has been seeking to narrow the gap with industry leader TSMC (2330.TW) in advanced contract chip manufacturing. Investors said they would also be closely watching for details of [USN:L1N44L00M TEXT:"Samsung's shareholder return policy"] during its earnings call later this month. ($1 = 1,339.5700 won)

item.title: French mayor caught in viral video clash says student protesters 'could be my children'
item.description: Bally Bagayoko, the mayor of the French town of Saint-Denis, faced police at a march in Paris, shielding young protesters and shouting "stop."
item.dc:creator: Layli Foroudi
item.content:encoded: In a video that has gone viral on social media, Bally Bagayoko, the mayor of the French town of Saint-Denis, stands facing police at a march in Paris on Tuesday, shielding young protesters and shouting "stop." Bagayoko said he has been supporting the students in his working-class Parisian suburb and on Tuesday was asking the police not to charge. "They had decided to charge and effectively go after the students, many of whom had shown no aggressive behaviour whatsoever toward the police officers," Bagayoko, who is part of the hard-left France Unbowed party (LFI), told Reuters in an interview on Wednesday at his town hall office in Saint-Denis, on the northern outskirts of Paris. In the end, the police fired tear gas at the group, including the mayor, he said. The wave of student protests, which began in [USN:L6N45M1EJ TEXT:"Paris' marginalised suburbs"], has been going on for more than two weeks and has exposed widespread public anger six months ahead of an election to replace French President Emmanuel Macron. There have been more than 6,000 arrests and dozens of student injuries since the protests began. Rights groups and unions accuse the police of using heavy-handed tactics against minors, including the use of batons, tear gas and non-lethal flashball guns. Authorities say hundreds of police officers have also been injured, schools have been burned or ransacked, and teachers and members of the public have been attacked. The town of Saint-Denis, where poverty levels are more than double the national average, was one of the first sites of student protests in late September over overcrowded and unsanitary classrooms, teacher shortages and unequal opportunities. "Protests are not new here, they happen at every start of the academic year," Bagayoko said. "The Republican promise (of equality) — in particular for the working-class neighbourhoods, and also rural areas — is not respected." He said the government should prioritise investing in education and levy heavier taxes on billionaires. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said on Wednesday that the government would review demands made by students and present proposals at the end of October, but gave no details. The government has suggested that LFI politicians were behind the protests, an accusation that Bagayoko dismissed as insulting to the young protesters. A father of four, he said that "the high school children who were in the street could be my children ... it is my responsibility to be at their side."

item.title: Venezuela's Maduro to face new US charges over alleged torture of Americans, official says
item.description: Ousted Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores are expected to face new criminal charges in the United States over allegations that Americans detained in Venezuela were tortured, a US official said on Wednesday.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Goudsward, Luc Cohen
item.content:encoded: Ousted Venezuelan President [USN:L6N44P07P TEXT:"Nicolas Maduro"] and his wife Cilia Flores are expected to face new criminal charges in the United States over allegations that Americans detained in Venezuela were tortured, a US official said on Wednesday. The new charges could come as soon as Thursday, according to the official, who was briefed on the investigation. Maduro, who led Venezuela for 13 years, and Flores were captured by the US military from their home in Caracas on January 3 and brought to New York to face drug trafficking charges. They have pleaded not guilty and are scheduled to go on trial [USN:L6N43O0Z4 TEXT:"starting June 1"], 2027. A spokesperson for the Manhattan US Attorney's office, which brought the charges, declined to comment. Lawyers for Maduro and Flores did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The possibility of new charges was first reported by CNN on Wednesday. Details of the new charges, including the identities of the alleged torture victims, were not immediately available. Maduro's tenure was marked by tensions with the United States. Washington accused his government of detaining Americans as leverage to extract concessions such as relief from financial sanctions. Americans whom the US classified as wrongfully detained during Maduro's tenure included five oil executives arrested on graft charges. They were [USN:L1N3120I8 TEXT:"freed in 2022"] in exchange for two of Flores' nephews who had been convicted in the US of drug trafficking. Others detained included two former US Army Special Forces members who were arrested in Venezuela in 2020 in connection with a botched raid aimed at ousting Maduro. They were [USN:S0N3BU02L TEXT:"freed in 2023"] as part of another prisoner swap. Since Maduro's capture, Venezuela has been led by his former vice president, Delcy Rodriguez, who has increased cooperation with the Trump administration. Maduro, 63, and Flores, 69, have been held in a federal jail in Brooklyn. Flores is due to appear in Manhattan federal court on Thursday to urge US District Judge Alvin Hellerstein to release her from jail before trial for health reasons. Prosecutors oppose her release.

item.title: Christian Dior board replaces two members ahead of new shareholding structure
item.description: French luxury company Christian Dior said on Wednesday it replaced two independent board members ahead of a change of shareholding structure planned by the family of billionaire Bernard Arnault.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: French luxury company Christian Dior (DIOR.PA) said on Wednesday it replaced two independent board members ahead of a change of shareholding structure planned by the family of billionaire Bernard Arnault. Xavier Musca, a former top executive at Credit Agricole, and Tony Estanguet, who led the committee in charge of the Paris Olympics in 2024, will replace Nicolas Bazire and Maria Luisa Loro Piana, effective immediately, the company said. The Arnault family, which controls Dior and French luxury behemoth LVMH (LVMH.PA) through its holding company Agache, said last month it plans to merge it with Dior. Agache currently owns 96% of Dior shares and 97.1% of the voting rights in Christian Dior and 6.77% in LVMH and 8.49% of the voting rights in LVMH. The merged entity will be named Agache and it will control directly 49.76% in LVMH and 65.55% of voting rights. The merger, expected in December, is set to include a tender offer for the 2.44% of the Christian Dior shares Agache does not own. The Arnault family will offer a price to be defined based on the LVMH share price.

item.title: Ronaldo hails Messi after Argentina great says he already misses national team
item.description: The Portugal captain set aside one of soccer's great rivalries to pay tribute.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Portugal captain Cristiano Ronaldo set aside one of soccer's great rivalries on Wednesday to pay tribute to Lionel Messi after the Argentine said he already missed representing his country following his emotional international retirement. Messi, 39, delivered one [USN:L1N45T01T TEXT:"final masterclass"] in Argentina's blue and white on Tuesday, scoring once and setting up two goals in a 3-0 friendly win over Benin before more than 85,000 fans at Buenos Aires' Monumental Stadium, where his farewell became a celebration of an extraordinary 21-year international career. "Yesterday was my last game, and I already miss wearing the blue and white. I know I'm making the right decision," Messi said in a lengthy Instagram post. "It's been an incredible journey, full of joy and also some sadness, but I know for sure that every step I took was worth it... "I don't want to forget Diego (Maradona), who put our country where it deserved to be and who, as I always say, I know helped us both by being here with us and also from heaven, with every step we took. "Thank you to the clubs where I played, for always respecting my feelings and allowing me to dedicate myself to my country whenever it was time to put on the national team jersey..." Messi captained Argentina to the 2022 World Cup title and Copa America triumphs in 2021 and 2024, while also helping them win the 2022 Finalissima. "I am grateful. I love you all very much; I'm going to miss you, and I will always thank you for having been by our side, by my side," the Inter Miami playmaker added. Messi and Ronaldo have vied for recognition as the greatest player of their generation throughout their illustrious careers, with the 41-year-old Portuguese forward among those to respond to the post. "Leo, after so many years of defending your country, you've made history that will last forever. I have the utmost respect for what you've accomplished with Argentina. A hug," Ronaldo said. Ronaldo, meanwhile, is [USN:L6N45S178 TEXT:"embroiled in a dispute"] with Portugal coach Jorge Jesus following his abrupt departure from the national team's training camp.

item.title: Britain's BBC, Channel 4 discuss broader tie-up to cut costs, sources say
item.description: Britain's BBC and Channel 4 have held preliminary talks with the government about a broader tie-up of some operations, two people with direct knowledge of the discussions said, in a potential shake-up of the country's public broadcasters.
item.dc:creator: Amy-Jo Crowley
item.content:encoded: Britain's BBC and Channel 4 have held preliminary talks with the government about a broader tie-up of some operations, two people with direct knowledge of the discussions said, in a potential shake-up of the country's public broadcasters. One option under discussion would combine Channel 4's advertising operations, channels including E4 and Film4, and its video-on-demand services, with UKTV, a commercial subsidiary of the BBC, the people told Reuters. A merged entity could be equally owned by the BBC and Channel 4 and represent a broader tie-up than the one previously indicated by BBC Director General Matt Brittin to include Channel 4 content in the BBC's iPlayer, the people said. The talks could intensify next year depending on what progress the BBC makes towards [USN:L8N43G0OI TEXT:"a new funding deal"] with the government, one of the people said, adding that the assets included in the potential joint venture could be expanded. The joint venture under consideration would not include the Channel 4 flagship broadcast channel, which could benefit from fees from the joint venture, the people said. The move would be aimed at cutting costs and helping secure the future of the public broadcasters as linear viewing declines and larger streaming companies [USN:L6N43U0UJ TEXT:"account for more"] of global advertising spend, the people said. A BBC spokesperson declined to comment. "But as we've said before we believe increased collaboration between all (public service broadcasters) is vital to ensure the industry thrives in a highly competitive global market place," the BBC spokesperson said. A Channel 4 spokesperson said: "We won't be commenting on any speculation but we welcome and support greater collaboration between Public Service Media and strongly believe working together can strengthen impact, innovation and sustainability in UK broadcasting. Channel 4 and the BBC already have a successful commercial relationship, involving ad sales for UKTV and the carriage of U on 4Streaming." Channel 4 is government-owned but funded by advertisements, while the publicly owned BBC is mainly funded by a licence paid by TV-watching households. The talks involve UK Government Investments (UKGI), the entity responsible for managing publicly owned assets such as Channel 4, the people said. The plans could help Channel 4 and the BBC save costs, bringing some operations under one management and gaining a bigger slice of a consolidating market, the people said. UKGI declined to comment. DISCUSSING A DEEPER TIE-UP If it went ahead, such a move would represent one of the biggest shake-ups for the broadcasters since Britain [USN:S8N31X084 TEXT:"scrapped"] plans to sell Channel 4 in 2023. Former Prime Minister Boris Johnson's government had announced the sale in 2022, triggering a backlash from lawmakers and the broadcasting industry. The two broadcasters had already been discussing partnerships around content sharing, such as a [USN:L8N45L0ZF TEXT:"potential plan"] to carry Channel 4 content on iPlayer. Channel 4 already carries UKTV content such as "The Office" and "Red Dwarf" on its streaming platform and manages ad sales for UKTV under a long-standing agreement. While it has ruled out merging with the BBC, it is open to sharing content on the iPlayer streaming service, Channel 4's CEO Priya Dogra [USN:L8N45L0ZF TEXT:"said at an industry event last month"]. Channel 4 and the BBC are pursuing cost-cutting, including through job reductions. The BBC [USN:L8N42P0X7 TEXT:"said"] in June it would cut 550 jobs as part of plans under [USN:SPN40B000 TEXT:"Brittin"] to save £500 million ($661 million) over the next three years. Channel 4, which cut its pre-tax deficit to £10 million in 2025, said last month it would cut about 340 jobs, representing more than a quarter of its workforce, in one of the biggest rounds of redundancies in its 43-year history. It also said it agreed a tie-up of its ad sales operations with Paramount-Skydance's Channel 5, another public service broadcaster. ($1 = 0.7569 pounds)

item.title: Metall-Tarifgespräche in NRW und BW enden ohne Fortschritt
item.description: In der Tarifrunde der Metall- und Elektroindustrie haben IG Metall und Arbeitgeber ihre ersten Gespräche für die rund 640.000 Beschäftigten der Branche in Nordrhein-Westfalen ohne greifbare Ergebnisse beendet. "Die Arbeitgeber haben heute kein Angebot vorgelegt", sagte der Verhandlungsleiter der IG Metall NRW, Knut Giesler, am Mittwoch in Düsseldorf. Dies sei enttäuschend. Zugleich bekräftigte er die Forderung der Gewerkschaft nach fünf Prozent mehr Lohn. Auch die erste Runde in Baden-Württemberg endete ohne Angebot der Arbeitgeber, aber mit mehr Übereinstimmung in der Beurteilung der schwierigen wirtschaftlichen Ausgangslage.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: In der Tarifrunde der Metall- und Elektroindustrie haben IG Metall und Arbeitgeber ihre ersten Gespräche für die rund 640.000 Beschäftigten der Branche in Nordrhein-Westfalen ohne greifbare Ergebnisse beendet. "Die Arbeitgeber haben heute kein Angebot vorgelegt", sagte der Verhandlungsleiter der IG Metall NRW, Knut Giesler, am Mittwoch in Düsseldorf. Dies sei enttäuschend. Zugleich bekräftigte er die Forderung der Gewerkschaft nach fünf Prozent mehr Lohn. Auch die erste Runde in Baden-Württemberg endete ohne Angebot der Arbeitgeber, aber mit mehr Übereinstimmung in der Beurteilung der schwierigen wirtschaftlichen Ausgangslage. Die nordrhein-westfälischen Metallarbeitgeber wiesen die Forderung als "schlicht wirklichkeitsfremd" zurück. Die Branche stecke in der schwersten Strukturkrise seit Jahrzehnten, sagte ihr Verhandlungsleiter Arndt Kirchhoff. "Unsere Unternehmen stehen unter einem extremen Kostendruck – und die Höhe der Arbeitskosten spielt hier eine entscheidende Rolle." Giesler hatte die Forderung dagegen als "moderat" bezeichnet. "In NRW muss keiner wegen eines Tarifvertrags Insolvenz anmelden." Zugleich will die Gewerkschaft aber auch mehr Sicherheit für Arbeitsplätze und Standorte. Bei "Boom-Unternehmen", etwa in der Verteidigungsindustrie, soll es eine tarifliche Gewinnbeteiligung geben. Bei Krisenunternehmen will die IG Metall prüfen, ob die Instrumente für Beschäftigungssicherung und Zukunftsinvestitionen ausreichen. "DIE UHR TICKT" Im Südwesten führt die besonders schwierige Lage der dort stark vertretenen Autoindustrie zu einer ähnlichen Sicht der Tarifparteien auf die Ausgangslage der diesjährigen Runde. Beiden Seiten sei klar, dass es keine normale Runde sei, sondern eine in Krisenzeiten, in der es auch um die Sicherung von Arbeitsplätzen gehe, erklärten die IG-Metall-Bezirkschefin Barbara Resch wie auch ihr Widerpart, Südwestmetall-Chef Peter Krause. "Die Uhr tickt zum Erhalt des Industriestandortes Baden-Württemberg - es liegt an den Tarifpartnern, schnell zu weiteren Schritten zu kommen", sagte Resch in Ludwigsburg und mahnte so wie Giesler die Vorlage eines Angebots an. Die Präsentationen zur Beschreibung der Lage der Industrie mit ihren 914.000 Beschäftigten im Ländle seien überraschend deckungsgleich gewesen, sagte Krause nach zwei Stunden Austausch. Man sei in einer Krisensituation. Beide Seiten müssten ihrer Verantwortung gerecht werden, Lösungen am besten im November zu finden. In der Sache gehen die Ansichten aber auseinander. Krause forderte niedrigere Arbeitskosten, um den Standort zu retten, und nannte die Lohnforderung von fünf Prozent "völlig überzogen". Resch sagte, ein finanzieller Verzicht der Beschäftigten löse keine Strukturprobleme. Unternehmer sollten aufhören, den Standort und die Arbeitnehmer schlechtzureden. Die Verhandlungen in den anderen Tarifgebieten für die insgesamt 3,7 Millionen Beschäftigten folgen in den kommenden Tagen. Baden-Württemberg und NRW wollen beide am 27. Oktober weitersprechen. Die Friedenspflicht endet mit dem Auslaufen des aktuellen Tarifvertrages am 31. Oktober. Danach sind Warnstreiks möglich.

item.title: UK PM Burnham's Labour Party faces challenge from Greens in Starmer's old seat
item.description: Andy Burnham needs to win over voters like tech worker Dani Arbid in a by-election on Thursday if he is to fend off a national threat to his Labour Party from the Greens — and the early signs are encouraging for Britain's new prime minister.
item.dc:creator: Alistair Smout, Ben Makori
item.content:encoded: Andy Burnham needs to win over voters like tech worker Dani Arbid in a by-election on Thursday if he is to fend off a national threat to his Labour Party from the Greens — and the early signs are encouraging for Britain's new prime minister. The vote for a parliamentary seat in the inner London electoral district of Holborn and St Pancras, made vacant by the resignation of former Prime Minister Keir Starmer, is a first test of whether Burnham can restore voters' faith in Labour, which saw its popularity among left-wing voters plunge over the war in Gaza. Many, like Arbid, turned instead to the Greens, helping them to their strongest result ever in local elections in May. Now, he says he is undecided on how he will vote in Thursday's by-election but welcomed Burnham's tougher [USN:L8N451191 TEXT:"messaging on Israel"] and his more ambitious approach to ties with the [USN:L8N45L1HL TEXT:"European Union"]. "It's very important to read the room, which I think the current Labour government is doing a lot better job at," Arbid, 38, told Reuters. "There is still room for Labour to kind of claw back some of those losses for sure." LABOUR TIPPED TO WIN BY-ELECTION Unlike the national picture, where Nigel Farage's Reform UK poses a serious challenge to Burnham, the by-election is mainly a contest between Labour and the Greens, with thousands of activists from both parties out canvassing in recent weeks. Burnham hopes to show he can consolidate the left-of-centre vote, strengthening his efforts to take on a British right now split between Reform UK and the Conservatives. But the by-election also offers him a chance to rob the Greens of the momentum they have built up under new leader Zack Polanski. Polanski himself is the Greens' candidate in Holborn and St Pancras but Labour's Sagal Abdi-Wali, a local council leader, is tipped to hold the seat for the governing party. Green gains in areas of London contributed to Labour's [USN:L1N41L05B TEXT:"dismal local election"] results in May, which helped set in train a process that culminated on July 20 with Starmer's resignation and his replacement by Burnham. Since then, however, Labour has rebounded in national opinion polls, while the Greens have suffered setbacks. At a conference last weekend, Green Party members voted to class [USN:L1N45Q059 TEXT:"Zionism as a form of racism"], drawing criticism from British Jewish groups, Israel and even some Green lawmakers. Polanski, who is Jewish, did not take part in the vote. Burnham's government, which has taken a more critical approach towards Israel and banned the [USN:L8N45007X TEXT:"import of goods from West Bank settlements"], said the Greens had overstepped a line. On Camden High Street, an area of London brimming with market stalls and popular with musicians, artists and tourists, Kamran Ahmed, a local resident who works in AI, said Polanski could have managed the issues raised at conference better. But on a local level he said the Greens had something new to offer, echoing frustration heard around the country that the previously dominant Conservative and Labour parties no longer have the answers. "Nothing is set in stone, but some of the mainstream parties have over-promised and under-delivered... If you take an area like Camden, it could benefit from some of the fresher thinking that the Green Party offers," Ahmed said. Damian Lyons Lowe, head of pollster Survation, said the seat was one of the Greens' top targets, and that governments rarely did well at by-elections. But the Greens' anti-Starmer message, which resonated so well in May, was being tested by Burnham. "Burnham has made direct appeals to Green-minded voters in terms of some of the things they care about," he told Reuters. "The Burnham vibe check is very different to the Starmer-led Labour government, and that's a problem for the Green Party."

item.title: Pharma lobby sues Trump administration over Medicare drug price cuts
item.description: The pharmaceutical industry's top lobby group on Wednesday sued to invalidate the Trump administration's efforts to benchmark US drug prices to lower costs overseas in the Medicare health insurance program, arguing that it is an illegal government overreach.
item.dc:creator: Michael Erman
item.content:encoded: The pharmaceutical industry's top lobby group on Wednesday sued to invalidate the Trump administration's efforts to benchmark US drug prices to lower costs overseas in the Medicare health insurance program, arguing that it is an illegal government overreach. The GLOBE rule intends to set hospital drug prices for Medicare patients. Its final version was published last week on exactly how a "most-favored-nation" pricing system based on what is paid in a group of comparable countries would be integrated in the Medicare Part B program. [USN:L1N45N0WX TEXT:"The rule"] is expected to have limited reach. CMS plans to waive it for manufacturers that have signed separate voluntary deals with the White House to cut prices for their drugs, and it could ultimately apply to as few as four drugmakers. The PhRMA lobby group filed its lawsuit in the US District Court for the District of Columbia against Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the US Department of Health and Human Services he runs, and the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services and two of its officials. The lobby group argues in its lawsuit that CMS, Medicare's regulator, has stretched the authority of a program to test new pricing ideas into rewriting Medicare's pricing structure without congressional action. Congress has given CMS "a little bit of authority to test models," PhRMA General Counsel Jim Stansel said in an interview. "Instead, CMS is doing exactly what Congress has declined to do multiple times over the last several years, and that's to replace the pricing structure in Medicare with a most-favored-nation structure." Stansel said that the lawsuit was important even with the limited reach of the rule because GLOBE could outlast the voluntary deals drugmakers have signed, and could extend to future administrations beyond Trump. Rachel Turow, an attorney with Skadden who is not involved in the lawsuit, said it can be viewed as an attempt to stop future price controls using similar mechanisms. If they don't foreclose the idea that you can use this process "to impose drug pricing controls, then they've basically opened the floodgates," Turow said. Medicare is the US government program that provides health coverage to about 70 million people aged 65 and older or with disabilities. The Department of Health and Human Services was not immediately available to comment on the lawsuit. In the finalized version of the rule, however, the agency argued that it was not overstepping its bounds, writing, "CMS is acting within a detailed, purpose specific statutory framework that Congress designed precisely for this type of model test." Trump has already signed deals with more than two dozen drugmakers, including many of the world's largest, such as Pfizer (PFE.N) , Eli Lilly (LLY.N) and Novo Nordisk (NOVOb.CO) . The final rule sharply reduced the government's projected savings from the model. HHS now estimates the program will reduce Medicare Part B spending by about $440 million over the 7-year model period, compared with roughly $11.9 billion projected in the proposed rule published last year. In 2020, PhRMA [USN:L1N2J324Z TEXT:"successfully sued"] to block a previous incarnation of most-favored-nation pricing, but that rule was invalidated on procedural grounds because the administration had rushed it out without giving the public a chance to comment. Also named in the suit were CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz, the agency's innovation center that is running the most-favored-nation pricing pilot and the director of that division, Abe Sutton.

item.title: Microsoft brings more AI to PCs as it challenges Apple
item.description: Microsoft unveiled on Wednesday an AI coding model that can run directly on personal computers and new security technology to prevent AI agents from accessing data without permission, challenging Apple's push to bring more AI into personal devices.
item.dc:creator: Stephen Nellis
item.content:encoded: Microsoft (MSFT.O) unveiled on Wednesday an AI coding model that can run directly on personal computers and new security technology to prevent AI agents from accessing data without permission, challenging Apple's (AAPL.O) push to bring more AI into personal devices. The software company also presented at the event in San Francisco a high-powered Surface laptop called Ultra powered by Nvidia's (NVDA.O) [USN:L6N42909E TEXT:"RTX Spark chips"]. Redmond, Washington-based Microsoft is seeking to turn Windows into a platform for AI agents to handle tasks such as writing computer code or tackling complex business projects on desktops and laptops. For Microsoft, the move represents a bet that some work that currently happens in its costly Azure cloud computing data centers can shift to high-powered Windows machines in businesses and homes, a market where the firm retains a stronghold — and where its customers foot the hardware bills. It is a market opportunity rival [USN:L6N45D0ZZ TEXT:"Apple is also chasing"] with new Mac computers. For Nvidia, cracking the Windows PC market could help it go after one of the last major markets dominated by Intel (INTC.O) and Advanced Micro Devices (AMD.O) . As a guardrail against increasingly autonomous AI agents that have created security risks, Microsoft said it was releasing Microsoft Execution Containers, a tool to prevent agents from accessing data and doing unauthorized tasks when running on a laptop or desktop machine. Anthropic, OpenAI and Nvidia will use the tools, said Pavan Davuluri, executive vice president for Windows and devices. “We needed to make the desktop the most secure place for agents to execute,” Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said. Davuluri said new tools would let IT departments set rules for agents and the Windows operating system would enforce those rules on each employee’s machine. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who joined Nadella on stage, said Microsoft’s new execution container technology, which goes by MXC for short, "is going to revolutionize how agents are built and deployed.” “Without it, (agents are) a complete nonstarter,” he said. Nvidia is [USN:L6N45K077 TEXT:"trying to prevent"] a repeat of the hack of AI hub Hugging Face, while Apple is looking to [USN:L6N45O14K TEXT:"tighten up the process"] for giving AI agents full access to a Mac computer's hard drive. AI MOVES TO THE PC Microsoft also unveiled AI models that previously required cloud access but can now run locally on high-powered Windows desktops and laptops, including Nvidia's open-source Nemotron model. Davuluri said a version of Chinese AI firm DeepSeek's V4 model can run on machines with at least 60 gigabytes of memory and outperform OpenAI's GPT-5 on some coding and reasoning tasks. Microsoft is taking a similar approach with its own Copilot AI assistant, splitting tasks between the cloud and individual laptops. “Copilot will still use the cloud for the hardest tasks, but for times when cost or privacy matter more, it can delegate down to local models that run directly on your computer,” said Microsoft’s Copilot chief Jacob Andreou. Davuluri also said Meta's (META.O) Muse personal assistant will come to Windows devices as a native app, using some of Microsoft’s new security tools, and that OpenClaw, the open-source AI agent system, can also work with those security tools. PRICE BARRIER One of the key challenges Microsoft and Nvidia face is the steep pricing of these devices after a memory-chip crunch drove up costs. The new Surface Laptop Ultra will start at $2,599 and rise to $5,899 for a model with a 20-core processor, 128 gigabytes of memory and one terabyte of storage. Apple's MacBook Pro with a 40-core graphics chip, 128 GB of memory and two TB of storage costs $6,700, although the machines are not directly comparable. Microsoft's entry-level Ultra costs more than Apple's $1,999 base MacBook Pro, but comes with 24 GB of memory compared with 16 GB on Apple's entry-level model. When Microsoft originally pitched the idea of running AI tasks on PCs two years ago to save costs, the laptops were mostly priced below $2,000, but Nvidia increased the price of an AI desktop machine called the DGX Spark by about 75% since its launch to $6,950 amid rising memory costs. Two years ago, "the software wasn't ready, but the hardware was. Now the software is ready and the hardware is too expensive to actually run it locally," said Anshel Sag, an analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy. "So it's becoming this thing where only the people who have the budget can really afford to run AI locally."

item.title: Trump rallies for Paxton in third Texas trip in a month as Republicans defend stronghold
item.description: US President Donald Trump made his third trip to Texas in a month on Wednesday to campaign for Republicans who now face unexpectedly tight midterm election battles as the party seeks to retain control of Congress.
item.dc:creator: Nandita Bose
item.content:encoded: US President Donald Trump made his third trip to Texas in a month on Wednesday to campaign for Republicans who now face unexpectedly tight midterm election battles as the party seeks to retain control of Congress. Trump appeared on stage in a packed San Antonio arena with Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton, who is locked in a close race with Democrat James Talarico. A loss on November 3 would complicate the party's path to retaining its slim Senate majority and mark a major setback in a Republican stronghold. Trump expressed appreciation for Paxton's loyalty. He endorsed Paxton in the primary after faulting the incumbent Republican senator, John Cornyn, for not supporting him during tough times. "He was with us all the way," Trump said of Paxton. "He's a fantastic man and what a job he's done." Paxton, called up on stage by Trump, thanked the president. "Mr. President I want to thank you for coming for me, for coming for us, and for coming for Texas. We are going to win this race," he said. Supporters, some waving cowboy hats, cheered for Trump and shouted "USA," drowning out several protesters who interrupted the event multiple times in a Texas city led by a Democrat. Trump said the protesters should "get the hell out of here." The rally was Trump's latest effort to mobilize his supporters for Paxton after staging an unusual [USN:L6N45M0UV TEXT:"mi"][USN:L6N45M0UV TEXT:"dterm convention"]in Dallas, in part to boost Paxton's campaign. But Trump has also publicly criticized his longtime ally, calling Paxton "a pain in the ass sometimes" last week before adding that Republicans "need Ken so badly." Trump's repeated trips to Texas are part of a broader push in Republican-leaning states, which were expected to be safely in hand but have instead become midterm battlegrounds. His 32-day campaign blitz has taken him through Texas, Oklahoma, Alabama, Ohio and Nebraska, while Vice President JD Vance has campaigned in Alaska. Trump and Vance carried all six states in the 2024 presidential election. Republicans are struggling as voters focus on high costs and the war with Iran, giving Trump [USN:L6N45R10Y TEXT:"record-low approval ratings"]. A Reuters/Ipsos poll completed Monday put his approval at 32%, with Democrats leading Republicans 44% to 37% among registered voters. Trump on Wednesday repeated comments he had made during a rally in Nebraska on Monday suggesting that Iran could attack Los Angeles or San Diego. Trump portrayed such rhetoric, which had drawn criticism from California's Democratic leaders and some Republicans, as underlining the stakes of the war he started on Iran. Trump surprised some Republicans in May by backing Paxton in a party runoff over Cornyn, whom party leaders saw as a safer bet. Republicans are now spending heavily to defend territory they once expected to win comfortably. Trump won the state by 14 points in 2024, but recent polls have shown Talarico ahead of Paxton. Republicans are also defending competitive House of Representatives seats in South Texas. Both Trump and Paxton attacked Talarico repeatedly in their remarks. For Trump, the stakes are also personal. James Henson, director of the Texas Politics Project at the University of Texas at Austin, said losing the Senate race would be "devastating for Republicans and devastating for Donald Trump" given his support for Paxton. "I think the president clearly will do a lot to try to avoid that outcome," Henson said. Trump's political operation has also poured millions into competitive House races. In San Antonio, Republican Carlos De La Cruz, an Air Force veteran, is running in a newly redrawn district, part of a Republican-led remapping that Democrats have called a partisan gerrymander. De La Cruz is expected to speak at Wednesday's rally. AN UNEASY ALLIANCE Trump relationship with Paxton has appeared awkward at times. Paxton was recorded telling donors that [USN:L6N45M0UV TEXT:"Republican candidates' numbers fell"] after the Trump-centered convention in Dallas, according to the New York Times, while Trump has publicly mocked Paxton's manner of speaking, clothes and appearance. "So to be honest with you, the numbers, when we did that convention, it dropped our numbers. Everybody's numbers dropped," Paxton said in the recording. His campaign has disputed suggestions that the remarks amounted to criticism of Trump. A spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment. A New York Times/Siena College poll released October 3 showed Talarico leading Paxton 51% to 45% among likely voters. Brandon Rottinghaus, a political science professor at the University of Houston, said rallying Trump's base was "necessary but not sufficient" for Paxton. "Trump's visits are a catch-22," Rottinghaus said. "The president can inspire as much as he can repel." Texas Republican Governor Greg Abbott, a close Trump ally who is also in a closer-than-expected re-election race, planned to skip Wednesday's rally, citing other campaign events. "My rallies are saving the Republican Party, again," Trump said in an all-caps post on Truth Social on Tuesday. Republicans are betting Trump can still turn out the voters who powered his 2024 victory even as his broader standing has weakened. The latest Reuters/Ipsos poll showed that just 24% of Hispanic voters approved of his performance. They were an important part of Trump's success in 2024, when he won nearly half the Hispanic vote, and are a bigger demographic in Texas than most states.

item.title: Israelis mark three years since October 7 as Palestinians mourn Gaza's destruction
item.description: Israelis mourned victims of attacks that set off Israel's assault in Gaza and plunged the Middle East into war.
item.dc:creator: Rami Amichay, Mahmoud Issa
item.content:encoded: Israelis gathered in silence on Wednesday in a kibbutz near the Gaza border that was overrun by Hamas militants on October 7 three years ago, mourning victims of attacks that set off Israel's assault in Gaza and plunged the Middle East into war. In the Gaza Strip, devastated by three years of Israeli bombardment, Palestinians sheltering among the ruins of destroyed cities recalled life before a war that [USN:L8N45L0U7 TEXT:"displaced nearly the entire population"] and tore apart families. The attacks of October 7, 2023, were the deadliest day in Israel's history. Militants led by Hamas killed 1,200 people and [USN:L8N45M1ZW TEXT:"took 251 hostages"], a cross-border incursion that traumatised Israelis who have demanded government accountability. Israel's subsequent bombardment and ground operations in Gaza have killed more than 74,000 people, including at least 1,400 killed in the past year since a US-brokered [USN:L6N45Q023 TEXT:"ceasefire"], which halted major fighting but has failed to stop Israeli attacks or secure the disarmament of Hamas. 'A VERY DIFFICULT DAY' In Kfar Aza, where Hamas militants killed dozens of Israelis before taking 19 hostages back into Gaza, residents held a vigil for those killed, standing in silence as a trumpet played a solemn bugle call. A resident read out a roll call of the dead. Zion Regev, a community leader in the kibbutz, said most residents remain displaced and have yet to return, the trauma of October 7 continuing to shape their lives. "This is the first time we are doing all the things here in the kibbutz," Regev said of the vigil. "It's a very emotional day, it's a very difficult day for our community, three years after October 7th." Elsewhere in Israel, protesters against what they view as a lack of accountability for the security failure gathered outside parliament in Jerusalem, blaming Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for refusing an independent inquiry into the attack. Some protesters held signs reading: "The people will remember October 7 on October 27," a reference to an Israeli general election 20 days away that is being viewed as a referendum on Netanyahu's long tenure in power. "We need the change and we need hope and we need to know that we have a government that cares about the public and doesn't work also only for themselves," said protester Shaked Arrad. Netanyahu has rejected blame for the security breach and resisted calls for an independent investigation. That has frustrated many in Israel, including families of those killed in the attacks, some of whom have [USN:L8N45F0EA TEXT:"joined the election race"]. In a statement released by his office, Netanyahu said: "The nation unites on this day in the longing for our dear ones." Referring to his country's ongoing attacks in Gaza, he added: "We will complete the mission: we have settled the score and will continue settling the score with all the murderers." Election polls show neither Netanyahu nor his main competitors would muster enough seats in parliament to form a coalition if a vote were held today. DISPLACED GAZANS RECALL LIFE BEFORE ISRAELI ASSAULT The anniversary is the first since the October 10, 2025, ceasefire deal, which has left Israel in control of around two-thirds of Gaza, where it has demolished remaining buildings and ordered residents out. Hamas controls the remaining third of the territory, a narrow strip on the coast where the [USN:L8N45L0U7 TEXT:"2 million population"] mostly [USN:L1N45O05B TEXT:"live in makeshift tents"] and bombed-out buildings. In the latest violence, Gaza medics said on Wednesday Israel's military had carried out air strikes in Beit Lahia in northern Gaza and in Khan Younis in the south, killing at least two Palestinians and wounding others. The Israeli military said it struck and killed two people it described as militants with Hamas, which did not immediately provide comment. The military did not provide comment on the strike in Khan Younis. Umm Mohammad, a mother of five displaced from Gaza City and now living with her husband and children in a tent encampment in Deir Al-Balah, said the war had ripped her family apart. "We were one happy family. The war displaced us. My son left Gaza, the other went to a separate tent, my daughters left with their husbands to other parts of the Strip and we rarely meet," she said. On this day, she said, "we recall how happy, despite all problems, we were before the war broke out, destroying everything we loved."

item.title: At least 32 killed in Ukraine, Zelenskiy condemns one of Russia's most 'vile strikes'
item.description: Russia pounded Ukraine with waves of missiles and drones in one of its most "vile strikes," President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said.
item.dc:creator: Olena Harmash, Vladyslav Smilianets
item.content:encoded: Russia pounded Ukraine with waves of missiles and drones in one of its most "vile strikes" on Wednesday, President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said, killing at least 32 people, including children, and damaging industrial facilities and energy infrastructure. The heaviest losses were in Pryluky in Ukraine's northern Chernihiv region, where a Russian missile destroyed a five-storey residential building. Ukraine's emergency service said on Telegram that the death toll in Pryluky has risen to 22 as of Thursday morning and two more bodies were discovered following a Russian air strike on an apartment building in the capital Kyiv, taking the toll there to four dead. Interior Minister Ivan Vyhivskyi has earlier put the country-wide death toll at 28, including 20 people who died in the Pryluky attack, including five children. On Wednesday evening, prosecutors in Kyiv said falling debris from a drone killed two people in a suburb. Zelenskiy said that 100 people had been injured throughout the country. The president noted that the attacks coincided with Russian President Vladimir Putin's birthday. "This is the kind of birthday present that Putin gave himself: the killing of children, the killing of people," Zelenskiy said in his nightly video address. In earlier online comments, Zelenskiy said civilians had also been killed in the capital Kyiv and in the central cities of Oleksandria and Kremenchuk during the massive attack. In total, Russia fired 70 missiles at Ukraine overnight — many of them high-velocity ballistic munitions — and dozens of Shahed attack drones, he said. "The Russians wanted to strike painfully and demonstratively. This was one of the most vile strikes." In Pryluky, an excavator and dozens of rescuers with shovels sifted through rubble at the site where several sections of the apartment block had collapsed. Emergency workers used ladders to get to the upper floors of what remained of the building, and brought out 15 survivors as they worked their way down through the rubble. Around 55 people were wounded in the town, regional officials said. "There's a lot of destruction, especially in the town centre," said Danylo Savenko, deputy mayor of Pryluky, who said he had run to an air raid shelter with his wife as soon as he heard the missiles flying. BIG JUMP IN REPORTED DRONE INTERCEPTIONS Russia's defence ministry said its forces had carried out a "massive strike" on military-industrial facilities in Kyiv and other Ukrainian regions, using high-precision land-, sea- and air-launched weapons, as well as drones. Ukraine's air force said it had downed just over 80% of the 46 jet-powered drones launched by Russia — an increase from recent weeks when air defences took down 50% to 60%. Since the summer, Russia has used increasing numbers of the new high-velocity drones in round-the-clock attacks on Kyiv and other cities, with Ukraine's air defences struggling to cope. The air force did not explain the jump in the interception rate and did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Zelenskiy said the Russian ballistic missiles remained the major challenge for Ukraine, adding that he and his team were "every day looking for Patriot (missile interception) systems that can and must protect people's lives". Ukraine received a new €1.2 billion ($1.34 billion) tranche from the European Union on Wednesday and will channel the funds towards defence needs, Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi said. The US-made Patriot system is the only weapon in Ukraine's arsenal capable of stopping high-velocity ballistic missiles. Global supplies have been drained by the Iran war and the Ukraine conflict. Russia's defence ministry said its targets included sites where Ukrainian defence company Fire Point manufactures and stores its Flamingo cruise missiles and medium- and long-range drones in Kyiv as well as regions of Kyiv, Chernihiv, Kirovohrad, Dnipropetrovsk, Poltava and Kharkiv. Last week Zelenskiy said Ukraine had fired its first domestically made ballistic missile in combat, produced by Fire Point. In an [USN:L1N45R056 TEXT:"interview"] with Reuters, he said he expected the company to have a longer-range FP-9 missile ready by the autumn. Fire Point has said that weapon will be able to reach Moscow. PEOPLE SHELTER OVERNIGHT IN KYIV METRO Zelenskiy said Ukrainian troops hit four targets in Russia over the past 24 hours, including two Russian oil facilities and a training ground in the Perm, Samara and Astrakhan regions. In the Reuters interview, Zelenskiy said Ukraine would hit Russia's energy assets in response to Moscow's escalating strikes on civilian infrastructure. Ukrainian officials and military intelligence shared warnings of the upcoming attacks on Wednesday, and many Kyiv residents took shelter in the city's underground metro stations. Several loud explosions reverberated through the capital during the night. In the part of Ukraine's southern Kherson region under Russian control, the regional Russia-installed governor said a Ukrainian drone killed two civilians in a car. And Russia-installed officials in Moscow-held parts of eastern Donetsk Region said three people died in Ukrainian attacks. ($1 = 0.8947 euros)

item.title: India among seven countries vying for 2036 Olympics, IOC says
item.description: A shortlist will be drawn up in March next year and some countries will progress to a strategic dialogue phase.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Seven countries, including India, Germany and Qatar, are in the running to stage the 2036 Summer Olympics, the International Olympic Committee said on Tuesday. Hungary, Turkey, South Africa and South Korea complete the list of interested parties, who are in preliminary talks with the IOC, with a shortlist to be drawn up in March next year and some countries progressing to a strategic dialogue phase. "Wherever the Games take place, one thing must never change: athletes have to be at the heart of everything we do ," said IOC President Kirsty Coventry. "That is why, for every future host, delivering the best possible experience for the athletes must always be the starting point.” India, the world's most populous nation, is attempting to land its first Olympics while Qatar, which has bid before with Doha, is campaigning to become the first Muslim-majority nation to host the world's biggest multi-sports event. Qatar staged the 2022 soccer World Cup. Hungary, which most recently bid for the 2024 Olympics, has never staged the Games while Munich, host of the 1972 Olympics, is Germany's candidate. ISTANBUL TRIES AGAIN Turkey's Istanbul has failed in five previous attempts while South Africa is hoping to become the first African host of the Olympics. South Africa has major event experience, having organised the 2010 soccer World Cup. South Korea has staged both summer and winter Olympics in Seoul in 1988 and Pyeongchang in 2018. Preferred hosts will be named after the dialogue phase in 2028 and a final decision is expected in mid-2029. Any other interested countries have until October 31 to come forward but new candidates are highly unlikely to emerge with less than four weeks before the deadline. Bidding rules changed under Coventry this year, adding the strategic dialogue stage and involving members more throughout the process. It is also very likely that more than one country will be named as preferred hosts, unlike in past votes where just one bidder was put forward by the IOC executive board. Los Angeles will stage the 2028 Summer Games and Australia's Brisbane will host them four years later.

item.title: Francis Halzen wins Nobel physics prize for Antarctic 'ghost particle' hunt
item.description: The scientist won for his work creating an observatory of ice to detect high-energy neutrinos.
item.dc:creator: Niklas Pollard, Johan Ahlander, Marie Mannes
item.content:encoded: The Belgian-American scientist Francis Halzen won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics for his work creating an Antarctic observatory of ice to detect high-energy neutrinos, elusive subatomic particles that can reveal otherwise inaccessible information about the cosmos. Halzen, 82, realised that pristine ice at the South Pole could be used to track such neutrinos, sometimes known as "ghost particles" for the way they pass through the Earth without a trace, only interacting with matter extremely rarely. "The messengers bring information from the cosmos," Eva Olsson, of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, told a press conference. "They open the door to distant galaxies and tell us about the processes of exploding stars." "It's a great relief for me because this was not totally unexpected, and around this time of the year I always felt miserable because I didn't win the prize and thought it was terrible for my collaborators who deserved it so much," Halzen said at a press conference. "So that problem is finally solved." HALZEN HAILED FOR DETECTING 'MESSENGERS FROM THE COSMOS' The interactions registered by the IceCube Neutrino Observatory provide information about how high-energy particles are created and may even reveal previously unknown phenomena, the Academy said. "We could catch them in ice, that was the goal," Halzen said of the years-long effort to construct the observatory, which he described as opening "a window on the universe." In 2014, the US-based Smithsonian magazine dubbed Halzen "Neutrino Man" when giving him one of its Ingenuity Awards, acclaiming him for an "amazing experiment (that) heralds the beginning of a new era in astronomy". It even published a comic illustrating his life: "How One Physicist's Pursuit of the Cosmos Took Off in Antarctica". The observatory – in effect a telescope that shows neutrinos instead of light – is set in a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice, which extends to a depth of 2,500 metres below the surface near the Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station. More than 5,000 sensors await blips from the nearly massless high-energy neutrinos, which unlike other particles do not lose energy or change direction, in the hope of tracing their paths back to exploding stars, gamma-ray bursts, and cataclysmic phenomena involving black holes and neutron stars. They can expect to register about one per day. Halzen, a professor at the University of Wisconsin–Madison in the US, first presented his idea in 1988 for capturing neutrino traces at the South Pole, but the project was not completed until 2011. "I have to emphasise how lucky I was because, when we started this project, everybody realised this was maybe a good idea, but very few thought it would work, including myself," Halzen told the press conference by telephone. Neutrinos are electrically neutral, undisturbed by any magnetic field, which means that, in contrast to electromagnetic waves such as visible light, the direction from which they arrive points directly back to their source. FRUITS OF HALZEN'S RESEARCH YET TO COME The observatory has determined that high-energy neutrinos originate within but also far outside our own Milky Way galaxy, setting in motion an interstellar quest to find the objects and processes that create them. Through the long winter at the South Pole, when bringing anything in or out is difficult as temperatures below minus 50 degrees Celsius (minus 58 Fahrenheit) preclude even aircraft landing, a skeleton crew of "winterovers" has to maintain the observatory. The station, home to many other activities, can house as many as 150 people and has an industrial kitchen, dining room, gym and even a greenhouse. Last week it celebrated the sun's return above the horizon after six months of night with a six-hole ice-golf tournament. An extension, IceCube-Gen2, encompassing 8 cubic kilometres of ice, is planned to become operational in 2033 and will be able to detect 10 times as many neutrinos, including much weaker ones. Halzen said the main fruits of his work were yet to be seen and that it was too early to say exactly what it could reveal about the universe. "This is a new way of looking at the universe, and it will take bigger telescopes, many more telescopes, to become real astronomy," he said. "And what this will bring is impossible to predict." WINNERS FROM EINSTEIN TO BOHR AND THE CURIES Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever congratulated Halzen on the recognition of "a life dedicated to unraveling the greatest secrets of the cosmos through its most minuscule manifestations". The physics laureate [USN:L8N45A0P9 TEXT:"receives"] an award of 12 million Swedish crowns ($1.2 million). Past winners include several other neutrino research pioneers, for instance Japan's Takaaki Kajita and Arthur McDonald from Canada in 2015. The [USN:L1N45R0AK TEXT:"Nobel Prizes"] were [USN:L1N45N0AY TEXT:"established"] under the will of Swedish inventor and entrepreneur Alfred Nobel, whose fortune was built in part on the invention of dynamite. Physics was prominent in Nobel's will and the prize remains one of the discipline's highest distinctions. Over the decades, it has recognised discoveries that have fundamentally reshaped humanity's understanding of the universe. Among past laureates are some of the most celebrated figures in science, including Albert Einstein, Marie and Pierre Curie, Max Planck and Niels Bohr, whose work helped establish the foundations of modern physics. The prize is presented in Stockholm on December 10, the anniversary of Nobel's death. ($1 = 10.0329 Swedish crowns)

item.title: Qualcomm and Arm kick off trial, potential for huge damages in focus
item.description: Chipmaker Qualcomm and chip tech firm Arm Holdings , , long at loggerheads, began another trial on Monday, with Qualcomm accusing Arm of withholding chip testing tools that were due under contract.
item.dc:creator: Tom Hals, Max Cherney, Stephen Nellis
item.content:encoded: (This Oct 5 has been corrected to say that Arm was seeking an 18,500% increase in royalty rates, not 1,800%, in paragraph 10.) Chipmaker Qualcomm (QCOM.O) and chip tech firm Arm Holdings (O9Ty.F) , , long at loggerheads, began another trial on Monday, with Qualcomm accusing Arm of withholding chip testing tools that were due under contract. Qualcomm also alleges that Arm leaked to the media its 2024 threat to terminate [USN:L4N3LZ01S TEXT:"a vital license agreement"] in a way that damaged discussions for a chip deal between Qualcomm and Meta Platforms (META.O) . In the lawsuit brought before US federal court in Delaware, Qualcomm, one of Arm's largest customers, is seeking to quit paying royalties — potentially worth billions of dollars — to Arm for up to five years. Qualcomm attorney Karen Dunn said in her opening statement that Qualcomm had been on the cusp of a deal with Meta when Arm notified Qualcomm that it was in breach of its architecture agreement and then allegedly leaked that notification letter to Bloomberg News. Meta became concerned Qualcomm would lose its license and Dunn told the jury that by the time Qualcomm secured the Meta deal the value had decreased by $170 million. “Delay is costly,” she told the jury. But Arm's attorney Gregg LoCascio told the jury it would learn that what really happened is Meta shifted to AI eyeglasses and away from virtual reality headsets and sought to adjust financial terms for Qualcomm chips as a result. “They were not harmed in the least,” LoCascio said. While a five-year hold on royalty payments sought by Qualcomm could be a major sales impact for Arm, Judge Maryellen Noreika is weighing whether to throw out that term of the contract, which could mean Qualcomm would be able to seek only a smaller amount of damages. In a related bench trial, Noreika also heard arguments over whether Arm has negotiated in good faith with Qualcomm for the next version of Arm's chip technology. Qualcomm's agreement with Arm runs through 2033. Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon testified during the bench trial portion of Monday's proceedings, during which Qualcomm's attorney returned repeatedly to a chart that showed Arm was seeking an increase of 18,500% in its royalty payments between version 9 and version 10 of its computing architecture. During a cross-examination, Arm's attorney pressed Amon on whether Qualcomm was aiming to get Arm to stick to pricing in a 2013 architecture licensing deal that capped royalties at $1.88 per chip for any chip with at least five central processor cores. Arm’s attorney asked Amon whether that agreement, which dates from an era of smaller smartphone chips, was under-priced in 2026’s market, where some data center chips have 288 central processor cores. The attorney asked Amon if the deal structure means that Qualcomm would be paying royalties for five central processor cores on larger chips and “getting 283 for free.” Amon responded that “I don’t see it that way.” The five-day trial marks another stage in the contentious relationship between Arm and Qualcomm. Arm sued Qualcomm in 2022 alleging that Qualcomm had breached its contracts, though Qualcomm came away in 2024 with a [USN:L1N3NL0WF TEXT:"key victory"].

item.title: OFRBS Summary
item.description: Les valeurs à suivre à Paris et en Europe
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Les valeurs à suivre à Paris et en Europe Les valeurs à suivre jeudi à la Bourse de Paris et en Europe : Zone euro: Les ventes au détail rebondissent moins que prévu en août 6 octobre (Reuters) - Les ventes au détail dans la zone euro ont rebondi légèrement moins que prévu sur un mois en août, selon les données publiées mardi par Eurostat, l'office statistique de l'Union européenne. Allemagne: Baisse surprise des exportations en août 8 octobre (Reuters) - Les exportations allemandes ont baissé de façon inattendue en août, accusant un recul de 0,8% par rapport au mois précédent, selon les données de l'Office fédéral de la statistique publiées jeudi. Etats-Unis: Les responsables de la Fed divisés sur la justification de la hausse des taux-"minutes" WASHINGTON, 7 octobre (Reuters) - Les responsables de la Réserve fédérale (Fed) ont divergé le mois dernier sur le raisonnement justifiant de relever les taux d'intérêt, certains d'entre eux notant la nécessité de contrer le choc énergétique tandis que d'autres, plus conservateurs, ayant dit avant tout vouloir lutter contre l'inflation.
